summary:
Earth Jukebox is a 3D web map that turns real natural events into sound, so people can hear what is happening on our planet. We built it using live data from NASA EONET (wildfires, storms, volcanoes, floods, landslides, drought, ice and more) and the USGS earthquake feed, shown on NASA GIBS satellite imagery. Each event type has its own sound, generated live in the browser. Pitch follows latitude, loudness follows magnitude and stereo position follows longitude. Users can click an event, play events in time order, or sweep a line from west to east across the globe and hear what it passes.

Natural events are usually shown as dots on a map or rows in a table, which is hard to grasp and inaccessible to people who cannot see well. Sound gives a new way to feel the scale and rhythm of Earth’s activity. Earth Jukebox makes NASA’s open data more engaging for students, teachers and the public, and more accessible to everyone.
details:
Earth Jukebox is a 3D web map that turns real natural events (wildfires, storms, volcanoes, floods, earthquakes and more) into sound. It uses live data from NASA EONET, NASA GIBS satellite imagery and the USGS earthquake feed. Each event type has its own sound. Pitch follows latitude, loudness follows magnitude, and stereo position follows longitude. Users can click an event, play events by date, or sweep a line across the globe from west to east and hear what it passes. All sounds are generated live in the browser, with no backend.

Natural events are usually shown as dots on a map, which is hard to grasp and not accessible to people who can’t see well. Sound gives a new way to feel Earth’s activity and makes NASA’s open data more engaging for students and the public.

Built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Three.js, Tone.js and TopoJSON. Hosted on GitHub Pages.

Use of AI: Claude (by Anthropic) helped write and debug the code and draft this text. The concept, data choices and testing are our team’s. No NASA logos are used.
